newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Bank of Spain freezes rates to help peseta.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bank of Spain freezes rates to help peseta.

text.p: The Bank of Spain refrained from a cut in its key interest rate on Friday --despite persistently high unemployment-- in the hope of calming a jittery peseta.
Milder-than-expected inflation data on Thursday had raised market expectations that the central bank would sanction its second interest rate cut of the year.
Spanish consumer inflation fell to a 2.9 percent year-on-year rate in January, its lowest in 28 years.
But the central bank decided to leave its key money market rate unchanged at six percent, apparently concerned by the peseta's shakiness this year, economists said.

"The central bank's caution is due to exchange rates. As far as inflation goes, the Bank of Spain has more than enough room to lower rates," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at the Bank of America.

After months of firmness, the peseta's calm was shattered this year as leading European politicians and businessmen began to debate in earnest Spain's inclusion in Europe's common currency - a cornerstone of government policy.
The peseta began to fluctuate wildly, forcing the Bank of Spain into the market to buy it - after months of selling it against the mark to brake its advance.
So far in 1997, the peseta has strengthened to a peak of 83.27 per mark and then weakened to 85.20 per mark.
"The Spanish unit has traded with excessive volatility," said Craig Schute, fixed-income analyst at Bear Stearns in London. "That is going to be worrying the Bank of Spain."
Given the Bank of Spain's recent support of the peseta in the market, it was likely it would also hold its rate steady in an effort to shore up the currency, economists said.
"Perhaps the only impediment to lower rates was the peseta," another Madrid-based economist said.
Neither did high unemployment sway its decision.

The National Statistics Institute household survey said unemployment in the fourth quarter fell slightly to 21.78 percent from 21.90 percent. That leaves the jobless rate at about twice the European average.
Separately, the Labour Ministry said the number of registered unemployed rose to 14.07 percent in January from 13.82 percent in December.

"By lowering rates the Bank of Spain is going to help strengthen economic activity...which in turn will rub off on the labour market," Schute said. "But to make Spanish unemployment more competitive on an international basis there is a need for structural reforms."
Spanish unions and employers were meeting on Friday to continue talks on labour market reform in an increasingly tense atmosphere which might prompt the government to intervene.
"It looks like talks between unions and employers are going nowhere fast," Schute said. "The mixed (employment) figures are not going to help lubricate the talks."
